title: Mākena resort community EIS and remaining permits
summary: In August 2026 the Planning Commission accepted the Mākena project's environmental impact statement for 652 homes, 109 of them workforce units, with market-rate homes using private brackish wells. Staff said Land Use Commission, County Council and coastal permit reviews are still needed, and phase one comes back to the commission.

timeline.text: One commissioner said the EIS lacked plans for carbon and waste and would have preferred to defer it.
The applicant's attorney said the workforce units will be built on site to meet the county's affordable housing rule.
An applicant water expert said the local aquifer is now pumped at about one-third of its sustainable yield.
The applicant's attorney said salty leftover water from the treatment system would be reused for irrigation.
A testifier asked for a delay until the developer gives a site-specific plan for its system to take salt out of well water.
Community survey respondents worried the project would worsen limited resources, especially water.
Market-rate homes and irrigation would use private brackish wells, while workforce homes would use the county water system.
Phase one of the Mākena project would need a coastal-zone permit that comes back to this commission.
The planner said the applicant will start building the workforce units in the first construction phase.
The planner said the home count was cut 27% from the 900 units first proposed, after community feedback.
The Mākena project proposes 652 homes: 543 market-rate and 109 workforce housing units built on site.
A redesign of the south golf course cut its irrigated area by 15 acres, lowering its water use by 20%.
Parts of the Mākena project still need Land Use Commission, County Council and coastal-zone permit reviews.
Staff said accepting the EIS does not approve the project, and more permits are still needed.
